# restrict and Pointer Aliasing

## Thesis

**`restrict`** (C99) is a promise you make to the compiler: for the lifetime of that pointer, no other pointer in the same scope will access the same object. That promise unlocks vectorisation and load/store reordering. Break the promise and you get silent wrong answers — not a warning.

## Mental model

```text
  add(n, out, a, b) with restrict on all three
       → compiler may assume out[i] is never a[j] or b[j]
       → safe to keep a[i], b[i] in registers across the store to out[i]
```

Without `restrict`, a legal (if pathological) call is `add(n, a, a, b)` where stores to `out` change later loads from `a`.

## Worked example

Verified with **GCC 14.2** `-O3 -std=c11`.

```c
/* restrict.c — fragment */
void add_restrict(size_t n, double *restrict out,
                  const double *restrict a, const double *restrict b) {
  for (size_t i = 0; i < n; i++) out[i] = a[i] + b[i];
}

void add_alias(size_t n, double *out, const double *a, const double *b) {
  for (size_t i = 0; i < n; i++) out[i] = a[i] + b[i];
}
```

A microbenchmark on this box (`n=1<<22`, 50 repeats, disjoint buffers) printed:

```text
n=4194304 restrict_ms=16.66 alias_ms=6.76 out0=3.0
```

Treat microbenchmarks carefully: both versions already vectorise at `-O3` when buffers do not alias, so wall-clock can go either way depending on cache state. The value of `restrict` is the **permission** it gives the optimiser, visible in the generated assembly (`objdump -d`) more reliably than in a single timing run.

## Trap

**Lying with `restrict`.** If `out` overlaps `a`, the compiler may emit code that is wrong for that call. Never slap `restrict` on API pointers "for speed" unless the contract forbids overlap (document it).

## Boring rule

Use `restrict` on hot kernels where the contract is "distinct buffers", document that contract, and prefer sanitizers / tests with deliberate overlap to catch misuse. Do not use it as a general style pepper.

## Try this

1. Compare `add_restrict` vs `add_alias` assembly at `-O3` with `objdump -d`.
2. Call `add_restrict(n, a+1, a, b)` (overlap) and observe wrong results under optimisation.
3. Read how `memcpy` vs `memmove` relate to the same aliasing idea.

## Sources

- ISO/IEC 9899:1999 §6.7.3 (`restrict`)
- GCC manual: [Restricted Pointers](https://gcc.gnu.org/onlinedocs/gcc/Restricted-Pointers.html)
